Lecture 5 · Part 1The Heart & Pulmonary Circuit

Lecturer: Dr Shaoyu Wang, Senior Lecturer in Anatomy & Physiology, School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences.

Chambers of the heart

Four chambers

  • Atria — the 2 superior chambers; the collection chambers
  • Ventricles — the 2 inferior chambers; the pumping chambers
  • Ventricles are larger than the atria

Sides

  • Right side — deoxygenated blood
  • Left side — oxygenated blood

Great vessels

  • Pulmonary trunk → pulmonary arteries
  • Pulmonary veins
  • Aorta — to all parts of the body

Blood flow through the heart & lungs

Superior + inferior vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary trunk → pulmonary arteries → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta

Remember: the pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood — the only place in the body where that is true.

Blood supply to the heart itself

Coronary arteries supply the cardiac myocytes with oxygen. The right and left coronary arteries branch off the aorta.

Right coronary artery

  • Conus
  • Marginal
  • Sinus nodal
  • Posterior interventricular
  • Atrioventricular nodal

Left coronary artery

  • Anterior interventricular
  • Diagonal
  • Circumflex
  • Marginal

Cardiac veins

  • Coronary sinus → great cardiac, middle cardiac, posterior vein, oblique vein, small cardiac
  • Anterior cardiac veins

Conduction system

SA node → AV node → bundle of His → right and left bundle branches → Purkinje fibres

Arteries · 1From the Aorta to the Neck

Branches off the aortic arch

Right side

  • Brachiocephalic trunk, which divides into:
    • Right common carotid artery
    • Right subclavian artery → right vertebral artery

Left side

  • Left common carotid artery — direct from the arch
  • Left subclavian artery → left vertebral artery
Exam point: the right common carotid arises from the brachiocephalic trunk, but the left common carotid comes straight off the arch. There is no left brachiocephalic artery.

Common carotid arteries

  • Ascend superiorly, lateral to the trachea and oesophagus
  • Bifurcate into 2 branches at the superior margin of the thyroid cartilage — the C3 vertebral level — giving the internal carotid and external carotid arteries
  • Contain the carotid body and carotid sinus near the bifurcation
Function: the carotid body is a chemoreceptor and the carotid sinus is a baroreceptor — one senses blood chemistry, the other blood pressure.

Arteries · 2Internal Carotid & the Circle of Willis

Internal carotid artery

  • Ascends in the carotid sheath, travelling posteriorly and laterally to the ECA after the bifurcation
  • Gives off no branches in the neck
  • Enters the skull via the carotid canal
  • Travels anteromedially through the carotid canal
  • Passes along the superior aspect of foramen lacerum into the posterior part of the cavernous sinus
  • Runs superiorly and anteriorly through the cavernous sinus along the medial part of the greater wing of the sphenoid
  • Turns abruptly posteriorly and superiorly to pass the anterior clinoid process and pierce the dural roof of the cavernous sinus
  • Splits into 2 terminal branches at the optic chiasma → middle cerebral artery and anterior cerebral artery
Four segments of the ICA, in order
CervicalPetrousCavernousCerebral
Revision question — “what artery passes through foramen lacerum?” The answer expected is the internal carotid artery, but note the wording on the slide: it passes along the superior aspect of the foramen rather than descending all the way through it. In life the inferior part is plugged with cartilage, so nothing passes completely through foramen lacerum.

Circle of Willis

Contributions

  • Right and left internal carotid arteries
  • Basilar artery — formed when the vertebral arteries join, after passing through the foramen magnum

Purpose

  • Provides resilient blood supply to the brain — an anastomosis, so if one feeding vessel is blocked, flow can still reach the territory from another direction

Arteries · 3External Carotid Artery

  • Ascends superiorly and posteromedially from the bifurcation, posterior to sternocleidomastoid
  • Travels posterior to the ramus of the mandible
#BranchKey course pointsSupplies
1Superior thyroidAnteriorly, at the level of the greater cornu of hyoid; 2 branches — one inferiorly along thyrohyoid to the upper thyroid lobe, one through the thyrohyoid membrane to the larynxSuperior ⅔ of the thyroid gland, larynx, SCM, pharynx
2Ascending pharyngealThe smallest branch; medially, then superiorly between the internal carotid and the pharynx; anastomoses with the ascending cervical arteryPharynx, superior constrictor, middle ear, dura of the posterior cranial fossa
3LingualAnteriorly at the greater horn of hyoid; passes deep (medial) to the hypoglossal nerve and hyoglossus; gives suprahyoid, dorsal lingual, deep lingual and sublingual branchesTongue, floor of mouth, suprahyoid muscles
4FacialAround the inferior border of the mandible, deep to digastric and stylohyoid; wraps around the submandibular gland; crosses the face diagonally; ends as the angular arteryFace, lips, nose, nasal septum, soft palate, tonsils, pharynx, submandibular gland
5OccipitalPosterosuperiorly, deep to the posterior belly of digastric; crosses the internal carotid, IJV, CN X and CN XI; passes between the transverse process of C1 and the mastoid processOccipital scalp, SCM
6Posterior auricularSuperiorly within the submandibular triangle to the parotid, then between parotid and styloid process to the auricle; anastomoses with the occipital arteryTympanic cavity, auricle, skin, parotid gland
7MaxillaryTerminal branch — see the next sectionDeep face, teeth, dura, palate, nasal cavity
8Superficial temporalTerminal branch — arises in the parotid, gives the transverse facial artery, crosses the zygomatic arch anterior to the auriculotemporal nerveSkin and muscles of the lateral face and scalp, parotid gland, TMJ
Mnemonic: Some Anatomists Like Freaking Out Poor Medical Students — Superior thyroid, Ascending pharyngeal, Lingual, Facial, Occipital, Posterior auricular, Maxillary, Superficial temporal.
Watch the numbering: this lecture calls the facial artery the 4th branch of the ECA. The scalp & facial nerve lecture calls it the 3rd branch. Both are defensible — counting every branch in order gives 4th, while counting only the anterior branches (superior thyroid, lingual, facial) gives 3rd. For a DOH255 answer, go with this lecture’s ordering and say “4th branch of the ECA, 3rd of the anterior branches”.

Branch-by-branch detail

Clinically: the facial artery and facial vein have opposite relationships to the submandibular gland — the artery grooves the deep (medial) surface of the gland while the vein runs superficial (lateral) to it. That is a favourite exam question.

Arteries · 4The Maxillary Artery

  • Terminal branch of the ECA
  • Branches anteriorly and anteromedially before dividing within the parotid gland
  • Split into 3 parts — the first two in the infratemporal fossa
The three parts, in order
Mandibular (bony)Pterygoid (muscular)Pterygopalatine
The pattern is the point: part 1 branches all enter bone, part 2 branches all supply muscle, part 3 branches all accompany CN V2. If you remember that, you can reconstruct most of the table.

Part 1 — Mandibular (bony) part

BranchRouteSupplies
Inferior alveolarGives lingual and mylohyoid branches before entering the mandibular canal; terminal branches are the incisive and mentalMandibular teeth, gingiva, lingual mucous membrane, mylohyoid, chin
Anterior tympanicThrough the petrotympanic fissure, with the chorda tympaniMiddle ear
Deep auricularThrough the wall of the external acoustic meatus; branch to the TMJTMJ, lateral tympanic membrane, skin of the EAM
Middle meningealThrough foramen spinosum to the middle cranial cavity — the auriculotemporal nerve forms a loop around itBones of the cranial vault, dura of the anterior and middle cranial fossae
Accessory meningealThrough foramen ovale to the middle cranial fossaMedial and lateral pterygoid, tensor veli palatini, sphenoid bone, dura, trigeminal ganglion

Part 2 — Pterygoid (muscular) part

BranchRouteSupplies
MassetericThrough the mandibular notchMasseter, TMJ
Deep temporalAnterior, middle and posterior branches, deep to temporalisTemporalis
Lateral pterygoidRuns directly to the muscleLateral pterygoid
Medial pterygoidRuns directly to the muscleMedial pterygoid
BuccalAccompanies the buccal nerveBuccal mucosa and skin, buccinator

Part 3 — Pterygopalatine part

BranchRouteSupplies
Posterior superior alveolarThrough the pterygomaxillary fissureMaxillary molars and premolars, gingiva, maxillary sinus
InfraorbitalThrough the infraorbital fissure, along the infraorbital groove and canal, exiting via the infraorbital foramen; gives the anterior and middle superior alveolar branchesMaxillary anterior teeth, cheek, upper lip, lower eyelid
Descending palatineGreater palatine → greater palatine foramen; lesser palatine → lesser palatine foramen; an anastomosing branch runs via the incisive canal to join the sphenopalatine arteryRoof of the hard palate, inferior meatus, palatine gingiva, soft palate, nasal septum
SphenopalatineThrough the sphenopalatine foramen to the nasal cavity; gives posterior lateral nasal branches and ends as posterior septal branchesFrontal, maxillary, ethmoid and sphenoid sinuses; nasal conchae and septum
Artery of the pterygoid canalThrough the pterygoid canalPharyngotympanic tube, tympanic cavity, upper pharynx
PharyngealThrough the palatovaginal canalNasopharynx, sphenoid sinus, pharyngotympanic tube
Dental relevance: the maxillary artery supplies essentially every tooth — the inferior alveolar for the mandibular arch, and the posterior superior alveolar plus the anterior and middle superior alveolar (from the infraorbital) for the maxillary arch.

VeinsVenous Return from Head & Neck

Tributaries of the superior vena cava

  • The right and left brachiocephalic veins drain directly into the SVC
  • Draining into the brachiocephalic veins: internal jugular, external jugular, subclavian and azygos veins

Dural venous drainage

  • All sinuses drain into the confluence of sinuses, located around the internal occipital protuberance — except the superior and inferior petrosal
  • From the confluence, blood enters the right or left transverse sinus
  • Transverse sinus → sigmoid sinus → through the jugular foramen → internal jugular vein
  • The inferior petrosal sinus drains directly into the IJV
  • The superior petrosal sinus drains into the transverse sinus

Cavernous sinus

  • A paired venous plexus (right and left) that communicate with each other
  • Located either side of the sella turcica

Communications

  • Angular vein via the ophthalmic veins
  • Pterygoid venous plexus via the inferior ophthalmic vein
  • The other dural venous sinuses

Relationships

  • CN III, IV, VI and V2
  • Internal carotid artery
Danger triangle: because the facial vein connects to the cavernous sinus through the ophthalmic veins and these veins are valveless, infection from the area between the corners of the mouth and the bridge of the nose can spread backwards and cause cavernous sinus thrombosis.

Pterygoid venous plexus

  • A venous network within the infratemporal fossa
  • Located partly between temporalis and lateral pterygoid, and partly between the medial and lateral pterygoid muscles

Tributaries

  • Sphenopalatine, deep temporal, masseteric, buccinator
  • Posterior, middle and anterior superior alveolar veins
  • Deep facial, inferior alveolar, infraorbital
  • Parotid gland, inferior ophthalmic, vein of the pterygoid canal

Drainage

  • Posteriorly: maxillary vein → retromandibular vein
  • Anteriorly: deep facial vein → facial vein
  • Communicates with the cavernous sinus
Dental relevance: this plexus sits right where an inferior alveolar nerve block is placed — puncturing it is the usual cause of a haematoma after a failed IANB.

Named veins of the face and neck

VeinOrigin & courseReceivesDrains into
FacialDescends obliquely from the root of the nose towards the inferior border of the mandibular body; runs laterally over the submandibular glandAngular, external nasal, superior and inferior labial, parotid, peritonsillar, submental, submandibularCommon facial vein → IJV
RetromandibularFormed in the parotid gland from the maxillary + superficial temporal veins; deep to the facial nerve, superficial to the ECAMaxillary vein (pterygoid plexus), infraorbital, superficial temporalAnterior division joins the facial vein → common facial → IJV; posterior division joins the posterior auricular → EJV
LingualBegins on the dorsolateral tongue (dorsal + deep lingual veins) and floor of mouth (sublingual vein); the two join between hyoglossus and genioglossusDorsal lingual, deep lingual, sublingualCommon facial vein → IJV
Internal jugularBegins at the base of the skull inferior to the jugular foramen; initially posterior to the ICA, CN IX, X and XI; then lateral (superficial) to the ICA within the carotid sheathSigmoid sinus, common facial, pharyngeal, superior thyroid, middle thyroidSubclavian → brachiocephalic → SVC
External jugularBegins near the angle of the mandible from the posterior division of the retromandibular + posterior auricular veins; descends obliquely, deep to platysma, superficial to SCMPosterior division of retromandibular, posterior auricular, anterior jugularSubclavian → brachiocephalic → SVC
Anterior jugularFrom the confluence of superficial submandibular veins near the hyoid, just lateral to the midline; runs inferiorly between the midline and the anterior margin of SCMSuperficial submandibular veinsEJV, occasionally the subclavian vein

LymphaticsLymphatic Drainage

  • Lymph vessels collect fluid from the capillary bed (interstitial fluid), along with cells, cell products, debris and pathogens
  • Pathway: lymph → lymph nodes (containing lymphocytes and macrophages, which filter the fluid) → lymph vessels → lymph trunks → subclavian vein
  • Normal lymph nodes are 0.1–0.2 cm
  • Enlargement suggests infection or lymph node metastasis

Lymph node groups

Superficial cervical nodes

  • Occipital
  • Post-auricular
  • Pre-auricular
  • Submandibular
  • Submental

Deep cervical nodes

  • Jugulodigastric
  • Jugulo-omohyoid

Systematic palpation

Why it matters in dentistry: examining the cervical nodes is part of every routine extra-oral exam. A persistently enlarged, hard or fixed node is a red flag that needs referral.

RevisionThe Lecturer’s Own Questions

These are the revision questions from the final slide — work through them before the exam.

  • Describe the lingual artery.
  • Describe the maxillary artery.
  • Discuss the facial artery and vein in terms of their location relative to the submandibular gland.
  • What artery passes through foramen lacerum?
  • Where does the common carotid bifurcate into the ICA and ECA?
  • Discuss the circle of Willis.
  • Where is the cavernous sinus located, and why is managing an infection close to the danger triangle so important?
